tagline: The spotted hunter of the Antarctic pack ice
summary: A long, sinuous, spotted seal with a huge head, at the top of the Antarctic food web. It eats almost anything from krill to penguins and young seals, sieving small prey through interlocking cheek teeth, and it roams thousands of kilometres between the pack ice and the subantarctic islands.
ability: teeth that both seize penguins and sieve krill

stats.size: Females up to about 3.8 m and over 500 kg; males smaller, about 3 m and 300 kg
stats.depth: Usually short, shallow dives (on average about 30 m and 3 minutes); one dive recorded to 1,256 m
stats.range: Around Antarctica's pack ice and the Southern Ocean, reaching the subantarctic islands, especially in winter
stats.diet: Krill, fish, squid, penguins and other seabirds, and seals, including crabeater and fur seal pups

facts.title: Bigger females
facts.text: Adult females measured at Cape Shirreff, Antarctic Peninsula, averaged 454 kg against 302 kg for males, about 50% heavier. That makes the leopard seal one of the most extreme cases of females outsizing males among marine mammals.

facts.title: Two ways to eat
facts.text: Captive leopard seals catch small prey by suction, then force the water back out through their cheek teeth, whose cusps interlock to form a sieve. The same jaws seize and shake penguins.

facts.title: A shallow diver, with one surprise
facts.text: Tagged adults at Cape Shirreff made dives averaging about 29 m and 3 minutes. One male, however, dived to 1,256 m for 25 minutes, far deeper than the previous record of 425 m.

facts.title: Penguin specialists, sometimes
facts.text: Leopard seals are generalists, eating krill, fish, seals and penguins. At Bird Island, South Georgia, they have been estimated to take 16–20% of the small local gentoo penguin population.

facts.title: Long-distance wanderers
facts.text: Seals tracked from Bird Island for an average of 294 days made trips of 100–500 km, some heading south to the pack ice, and travelled up to 1,950 km from the island. They spent about a quarter of their time hauled out.

facts.title: Slender-clawed water-worker
facts.text: Its scientific name Hydrurga leptonyx translates as 'slender-clawed water-worker', fitting an animal far more agile in the water than on the ice.

notes: Taxonomy per WoRMS (AphiaID 231417). The IUCN page blocks scripted access; the 2015 assessment (Hückstädt, assessed 20 January 2015) was confirmed through Crossref and the Least Concern category through SeaLifeBase and other secondary sources. The British Antarctic Survey's own leopard seal page could not be loaded (bot protection), so the BAS-led tracking study at Bird Island (Staniland et al. 2018) is cited instead. The 1,256 m dive is a single record from one adult male; typical dives are shallow. Size: ADW gives females up to 3.8 m and 500 kg; Kienle et al. weighed a 540 kg female. The filter-feeding evidence comes from captive seals in Australia. Leopard seals also wander further north (Commons holds photographs from Petone Beach, New Zealand, and from southern Chile and Argentina), but only the Southern Ocean is mapped as their range. The hero photo's Commons page gives no location. Category shelves left empty: none of the ocean shelves fits without forcing.
